title: shadow work, minus the jargon
hook: TikTok's favorite inner-work word comes from a Swiss psychiatrist, and from an older line about a speck and a beam
carry: what bugs me may be mine
tomorrow: what karma actually keeps track of

segments.voice: Yesterday: manifesting, and picture the wish, then the wall. Today, a word from the inner-work corner of the internet.

Shadow work. Journaling prompts, sixty-second videos, a workbook on every shelf. It sounds dark and a little mystical. It's neither, exactly. The word comes from a Swiss psychiatrist, and the idea is one you've already lived: the coworker who drives you up the wall for reasons you can't quite name.
screen: `SHADOW WORK.` → `DARK? MYSTICAL?` → `THE COWORKER WHO DRIVES YOU UP THE WALL.`

segments.voice: About a century ago, the psychiatrist Carl Jung used the word shadow for the parts of yourself you'd rather not claim. Not only the ugly bits. Anger you learned to hide, yes, but also ambition, softness, a talent that didn't fit the family. What we don't own, Jung thought, doesn't disappear. It tends to show up somewhere else, often in how strongly other people bother us. He called that projection. The idea is older than him. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus asks: "why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A speck in theirs, a plank in yours. So shadow work, minus the jargon, is one simple move. When someone gets under your skin more than they should, ask: is any of this mine? Not always. Sometimes people really are just annoying. And the higher self you hear about online is a looser idea, gathered from many places. Jung's own aim was plainer: to become whole, not perfect. For the light version, a notebook is plenty. For old, heavy pain, a good therapist is better company than any app.
screen: `THE PARTS YOU'D RATHER NOT CLAIM.` · `PROJECTION.` · `A SPECK IN THEIRS, A PLANK IN YOURS.` · `IS ANY OF THIS MINE?`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of someone who gets under your skin. On the second, name the trait that bugs you, in one word. On the third, ask, gently, whether any of that word lives in you, hidden or wanted. No verdict needed.
The shadow. The parts of you that you'd rather not claim, the dark ones and the bright ones. Sixth word.
Your line: what bugs me may be mine. Not always. Often enough to be worth asking. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 6 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT KARMA ACTUALLY KEEPS TRACK OF.`

howItsDone: People do shadow work with journaling prompts, in therapy (especially with Jungian analysts), and in reflection practices that ask what our strongest reactions to others reveal about ourselves.

what a scholar hears: Jung's shadow (German Schatten), projection and individuation, becoming whole; the speck and the beam is Matthew 7:3–5.

story.title: the doctor and the potion
story.text: A respected London doctor, tired of keeping his darker urges buried, mixes a potion to split them off into a separate man. It works. The other man is smaller, younger and free of every rule, and the doctor enjoys being him. But each time, the other man grows stronger, until one day the change comes without the potion. By the end, the doctor can't turn back.
story.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), often read alongside Jung's shadow

notes: New lesson (2026-10-06) from the research's proposed day 6 (Top 20 #11).

Jung's shadow summarized from Aion ch. 2 and related essays: the unacknowledged side of the personality, not only negative; projection as the usual way it shows; individuation as becoming whole. 'Whole, not perfect' is a fair gloss of Jung's preference for wholeness over perfection, not a quotation. A Jungian reader should confirm.
'About a century ago': Jung developed the shadow concept from the 1910s to the 1950s. Confirm wording.
'Higher self' is treated briefly as a looser popular idea from many sources (New Age, theosophy and others), not attributed to Jung, whose term was 'the Self'.
Clinical care: the teach says a therapist is better company for old, heavy pain, per the research's caution about borrowed clinical authority. No diagnostic language used.
Story: Jekyll and Hyde, told without the names in the spoken story; Hyde is described as smaller and younger in the novel, and the involuntary changes come late in the book. Confirm.
